examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070210/assets/67d511da69c49e77822011936522f2b236ccc0fa0e0fcd09ce26b428cc8f738a.png)

 

A plate with mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region $D$ enclosed between the curves $y=x$ and $y=4x-x^2$, as shown above. Given that the region has an area of $\dfrac92$ square units, find the moment of inertia of the plate about the line $x=3.$
examples.worked_solution:
The moment of inertia of a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ about an axis of rotation $l$ is given by

$$
I_l = \iint\limits_D \lambda (x,y) [r(x,y)]^2 \:\textrm{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda(x,y)$ is the mass density function of the lamina, and $r(x,y)$ is the distance from the line $l$ to the point $(x,y)$ on $D.$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 3, \:\: x \leq y \leq 4x-x^2 \right\},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070210/assets/6291950b5483f3c102df7249674412c7c11646409cb1b43df604de6bd5ace86f.png)

  

The distance between a point on $D$ and the line $x=3$ is given by

$$
r(x,y) = |x - 3|.
$$

Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda(x,y) = \dfrac{M}{\mathcal{A}} = \dfrac{2M}{9}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the line $x=3$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{2M}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{x}^{4x-{x}^{2}}|x-3{|}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2M}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{x}^{4x-{x}^{2}}(x-3)^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2M}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}(x-3)^{2}[y]_{y=x}^{y=4x-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2M}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}({x}^{2}-6x+9)(3x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2M}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}-{x}^{4}+9{x}^{3}-27{x}^{2}+27x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2M}{9}{[-\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+\frac{9{x}^{4}}{4}-9{x}^{3}+\frac{27{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{2M}{{3}^{2}}(-\frac{{3}^{5}}{5}+\frac{{3}^{6}}{4}-{3}^{5}+\frac{{3}^{5}}{2}) \\  & =2\cdot {3}^{3}M(-\frac{1}{5}+\frac{3}{4}-1+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{27M}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070210/assets/55a781e535e1b469bc5da659eff8f82afd27a1e8bb92ccd36c2fce5a9dd49b07.png)

A plate occupies the region $D$ enclosed by the $y$-axis and the lines $x=\frac{4y}{3}$ and $x=4-\frac{4y}{3}$, as shown above. The mass density function of the plate is $\lambda (x,y)=2-x.$ Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the line $x=2.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The moment of inertia of a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ about an axis of rotation $l$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function of the lamina, and $r(x,y)$ is the distance from the line $l$ to the point $(x,y)$ on $D.$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,\frac{3}{4}x\le y\le 3-\frac{3}{4}x},
$$

 

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070210/assets/1f332ebf554ac0e1b9e5099244aa50de0beef38c92efcba04e95e73abd21ecb6.png)

    

The distance between a point on $D$ and the line $x=2$ is given by

$$
r(x,y)=|x-2|
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the line $x=2$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)[r(x,y)]^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{3x/4}^{3-3x/4}(2-x)|x-2{|}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{3x/4}^{3-3x/4}{(2-x)}^{3}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2-x)^{3}[{\int }_{3x/4}^{3-3x/4}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2-x)^{3}[y]_{3x/4}^{3-3x/4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(2-x)^{3}(3-\frac{3x}{4}-\frac{3x}{4})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(2-x)^{4}\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}{[\frac{(2-x)^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}(0-\frac{{2}^{5}}{5}) \\  & =\frac{48}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
